newsitem.title: USA: US experts see limited Deng-induced market swings.
newsitem.headline: US experts see limited Deng-induced market swings.

text.p: The eventual passing of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping may usher in a brief period of uncertainty which could temporarily dampen the appetite among U.S. investors for Chinese assets, analysts said.
But any negative market impact from the 92 year-old leader's death would probably be short-lived given his presumably limited policy role, they added.
Speculation that Deng is gravely ill did rattle stock markets in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan on Monday.
But Chen Zhao, an economist with the Montreal-based consultancy, China Analyst called the impact "purely psychological."

Deng retired from politics in 1993 but is purported to have retained some form of influence. But Chen said Deng has not been involved in policy for three years, and China has already undergone the transition to "post-Deng" leadership.

Still, the markets could feel a few bumps to mourn Deng's passing when it happens, Chen said, because "It is unseemly in the Chinese culture to rally the market when a leader like Deng is passing on."
The stock markets in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan have been performing well this year, and any selloff would not last for more than a month or so, Chen predicted.

Among the markets of Chinese assets, the domestic A-share market is more likely to be rattled than the B-share market for foreign investors, said Tom Gong, a vice president at U.S. Securities and Futures Corp.
Indeed, on Monday Shanghai's A share index lost about 9 percent, compared to 7 percent for the B share index.

The Hong Kong stock market, which is highly responsive to U.S. interest rates, and the Taiwan market, which is driven by fundamentals such as export performance, are unlikely to be kept in check by Deng's death for long, Gong said.
The Hong Kong Hang Seng Index on Monday eased 0.32 percent and the Tawan's weighted index fell 0.59 percent.

If China's political and economic policies stay on the same course, as expected by most China watchers, the relief from uncertainties could kindle a "China investment fever" later this year, Gong said.
A money manager noted that the renewed interest in China began emerging since last year when U.S. investors felt more confident that Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule would be handled smoothly.
For all practical purposes, Hong Kong remains the main surrogate for equity investment in China, he said.
China has pledged to keep Hong Kong's capitalist system intact for 50 years after the territory reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1.
U.S. investors have also warmed up to China's Yankee bonds against the background of hearty demand for emerging market debt paper, traders said.
Spreads over U.S. Treasuries have tightened about 20 to 25 basis points since the start of the year, with its 10-year global bond trading merely 75 points over U.S. Treasuries, they noted.
Standard and Poor's said on Tuesday that it would keep the positive rating outlook on China in the event of Deng's death.
China's long-term foreign currency debt is rated BBB by S&P and A3 by Moody's Investors Service.
Elizabeth Economy, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the current Chinese leadership has shown a strong commitment to continuing the open door policy.

China's president Jiang Zemin and U.S. president Bill Clinton agreed on an exchange of presidential visits when the two leaders met in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Manila last November, and China has shown more willingness to drop many of its biggest trade barriers in order to enter the World Trade Organization, she said.
"All these things force the Chinese leaders to focus on the outside world," Economy said.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is to visit China on February 24-25 and Vice President Al Gore is scheduled to arrive in late March.
